newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finns swelter in decade's warmest summer.
newsitem.headline: Finns swelter in decade's warmest summer.

text.p: While central Europe fights disastrous floods, Finns in the north are sweating out their hottest summer of the decade.

Temperatures over 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit) have been registered even as far north as Pudasjarvi, close to the Arctic Circle, in what meteorologists on Wednesday called the warmest June-July stretch since 1988.
Summer averages in this chilly Nordic country, including night-time levels, are usually around 15 degrees Celsius.

"Tourists don't usually come here for the weather," said Pirjo-Riitta Vatanen, head of the Finnish travel promotion board. "But travellers returning to Paris from Finland have told our staff how wonderful it was to spend three weeks in shorts without ever putting on a sweater."
At Finland's northernmost weather station of Utsjoki-Kevo in Lapland, the mean July temperature has been 14.5 degrees Celsius, almost two degrees over the long-term average.
Rainfall is less than half normal levels and the growing season is ahead of schedule, although some crops in southwestern Finland have suffered from lack of moisture.
Dryness has mainly affected early maturing barley and sugar beets in the southwest, but crops further inland have fared better, said Olli Rantanen of the Agricultural Research Centre of Finland.
Finns have been flocking to packed beaches and onto pleasure boats, sometimes with tragic consequences: 71 people have drowned so far since the start of June, up from 46 last June and July.
But the bathers have not had it all their own way.

The warm weather has also aggravated thick blooms of toxic blue-green algae in Finland's thousands of lakes and coastal waters, prompting health officials to warn against swimming in many parts and to close many Helsinki beaches.
